# Layout, drawing and typography

::: {.doc-lead}
Arrange panels, draw annotations, and control the details of a figure.
:::

## Everyday editing {#everyday-editing}

Everywhere in Flux the pointer is a **crosshair** built to stay visible on any background — a
white halo under a dark core, with a small gap at the centre so the exact pixel you are
pointing at is never covered. Over anything you can click or select — a button, a layer, a
swatch, an object — it gains an accent dot, and it tightens while you press.
Text fields keep the I-beam; handles keep their resize arrows and pan keeps the hand.

Drag to move (with smart snapping and alignment guides), arrows to nudge, **Alt+drag** to
duplicate, **Shift+drag** to constrain to an axis. To move something to a **different
figure**, just drag it there: the figure under the pointer lights up, and releasing puts the
selection into that figure where you dropped it (groups and panel captions come along; one
Undo brings it back). **Ctrl+X** cuts, **Ctrl+C** copies and **Ctrl+V** pastes, so a cut in
one figure and a paste in another is the keyboard way to do the same thing. **Ctrl+G** groups
(**Ctrl+Shift+G** ungroups), **]** brings to front and **[** sends to back (with **Ctrl** they
move one step), **Shift+H** / **Shift+V** flip, **Delete** removes, **Escape** cancels whatever
you're midway through. The Inspector's Align row lines selections up, distributes them, and
sets exact gaps.

The blue key labels let you work without moving the pointer."><img src="/assets/media/docs/figure-property-menu.png" alt="Native property menu with geometry, content scale and axis-view controls." width="906" height="1078" loading="lazy"></a><figcaption>Press F for the selected object’s geometry and axis-view controls. The blue key labels let you work without moving the pointer. Click to enlarge.</figcaption></figure>

Press **F** with anything selected for the **property menu** — the fastest way to edit, built
for one hand on the keyboard and one on the mouse. It opens **beside the selection**, never on
top of it (when nothing fits, it takes the side that covers the least), and lays its groups
out in narrow columns — each row is a key and a name over its control — so nothing scrolls.
Opening a larger picker repositions the menu when needed to keep the selection clear.
Every hotkey is a **left-hand key** (`1`–`6`, `q w e r t`, `a d g`, `z x c v b`; `h` for a
plot's **content scale** or a text's **letter spacing**, and `n` for **paragraph spacing**),
so the right
hand never leaves the wheel: press the key to **arm** the row, then roll the **mouse wheel**
anywhere on the screen to adjust it (a slow roll moves one step per notch, a flick moves fast,
a trackpad scrubs; **Shift** ×10, **Alt** ×0.1; **↑/↓** step too, typed digits replace), and
press **Space** or **Enter** to apply — **Escape** reverts. A choice such
as font or alignment expands its options inline (wheel, **w/a/s/d**, **1–9**, or click); a
colour opens the **palette** — every row on one line, the whole grid in view — with the
full **spectrum** beside it (a saturation/value square and a hue bar, seeded from the current
colour), a hex field and an **eyedropper**; hovering a swatch previews it live, a click
applies it, and a drag on the square previews until you let go. The hex field and spectrum
follow the preview. The opacity slider under the spectrum is the *picked paint's* own
opacity — a fill picker sets the fill's, a stroke picker the stroke's (a text colour sets the
object's opacity) — and shows the selection's current value (or **mixed**).
Releasing the hue or opacity slider applies that adjustment and keeps the picker open so
you can continue tuning the colour.
The eyedropper samples a colour from your screen. On Linux it uses your desktop's
colour picker; **Escape** cancels without changing your artwork. If screen picking
is unavailable, Flux offers a magnified view labelled **Pick from Flux window**,
which samples only this window. A completed pick is one undoable change.
**Escape** or clicking outside dismisses an unchosen preview; an incomplete hex stays editable
until you finish it. The palette comes in
**collections** — Flexoki (the default), ColorBrewer, Paul Tol's colour sets, and your
project's own imported palette — as tabs above the grid; **Shift+Tab** cycles them. **Tab**
switches the grid to the **colormaps**: every map fluxplot ships (matplotlib, Crameri's
Scientific colour maps, Paul Tol, cmasher), by collection and by type, each with a preview
bar — pick a map and hover along its bar to take the colour at that position, **r** reverses
it. Or take the *whole* map: **x** or **y** (or the *along x* / *along y* buttons under the bar)
lays it across the element as a **gradient** along that axis — x left→right, y bottom→top — for
a shape's fill or stroke, a line's or arrow's stroke (arrowheads included), or a text's glyphs.
The map's colours are stored on the element itself, so the gradient travels into every export
(SVG, PNG, TIFF), headless render and exported deck exactly as drawn;
the menu chip and the Inspector swatch show the map and name it (`crameri.batlow · along y`),
and picking any plain swatch returns the element to a solid colour. Plot *parts* take solid
colours only. Settings → Figure chooses which palette and colormap collection a picker opens on. Hovering any numeric row and rolling the wheel edits it directly, so
the menu works with the mouse alone as well; **s** searches the properties. It carries the
essentials (position, size with **aspect lock**, rotation, opacity) plus the deep cuts: dashed
strokes with dash/gap control, **arrowheads** on lines *and* open paths (filled or V-line,
sized, with round/flat/square caps), **corner radius** on rectangles *and* paths,
no-fill/no-stroke, separate **fill opacity** (**b**) and **stroke opacity** (**t**) — each
independent of the object's **opacity**, which multiplies both — text styling — and **save as
preset** for anything you want to reuse. The
right rail carries the same properties (fill, stroke and text colours with their palette
names, sizes, stroke widths, arrowheads), so the menu is a choice, not a requirement.

Numeric fields accept expressions such as `240/2` and display fractional values even when
the normal wheel increment is a whole unit. Drag a field’s label to scrub, or click
its input and type. A scrub or a continuous text/property edit is one undo step; **Escape**
cancels the current preview. Mixed selections show **Mixed** and how many objects a property
can change. Locked or hidden objects, including members of a locked or hidden group, stay
unchanged while you edit the rest of a selection.

In **Layers**, **Ctrl/⌘+click** toggles objects and **Shift+click** selects a range. With a row
focused, **↑/↓** moves through the list, **Home/End** reaches either end, **Shift+↑/↓** extends
the selection, and **F2** renames. A group opens or closes with **→/←**. Locks inherited from
a parent group explain which group must be unlocked.

## Resizing a figure {#resizing-a-figure}

Click the figure’s title above its frame, then drag an edge or corner of the frame. The
handles stay the same size on screen as you zoom. **Shift** preserves the frame’s original
aspect ratio. The Inspector shows the new dimensions during the drag; **Escape** restores
the original boundary, and a completed resize is one undo step.

Resizing the frame changes the export boundary. Your plots, text and shapes retain their
size and world position. Moving a left or top edge moves the boundary around the artwork;
elements and ruler guides adjust their local coordinates to stay in place. Artwork outside
the new frame remains in the project and reappears if you enlarge the boundary again.
Dragging the title still moves the whole figure. Slides use a shared deck stage size.

**Resizing a plot and its content scale.** Resizing a placed plot changes its axes and data
area but keeps its text and line widths at their true point size, the way changing a
figure's size in matplotlib does. The Inspector's **Content scale** (or the **K** scale tool)
is the other dial: it makes the plot's text and lines bigger or smaller inside the same box.
Pictures that have no text or lines, such as a PNG saved inside an SVG, have nothing for
content scale to change, so the Inspector says so instead of showing the field. Resize the
box to make them bigger.

## Drawing {#drawing}

The shape tools do what you expect; the **pen** (P) is placement-assisted: click to place
points; a ring appears when you're close enough to your first point to **close** the shape;
**Shift** constrains segments to 0/45/90°; dashed guides snap to alignments with earlier
nodes, and tick marks snap **equal edge lengths** — perfect squares and 45-45-90 triangles
from sloppy clicks. **Enter** finishes an open curve; while the background grid is showing,
the pen snaps to its vertices.

**Double-click a path** (or press **Enter** on it) to edit its nodes. Inside node-edit:
**v** moves nodes (**Shift+drag** constrains along the axes or the flanking tangents),
**p** continues drawing — connect to an endpoint to extend or merge the path — **d** deletes
nodes, and **Ctrl+drag** on a segment **bends** it. The Inspector's *Closed path* checkbox
opens or closes any path.

## Arranging text in its box {#arranging-text-in-its-box}

Press **T**, then either **click** for a label — the box hugs whatever you type on one line —
or **drag** out a box for a paragraph: the text wraps at the width you drew and the box grows
downward as you type. Every text box has a **sizing** mode you can change later — *Auto*
hugs, *Auto H* wraps at the box width and grows downward, *Fixed* keeps both dimensions — and
everything below arranges the text **inside** that box.

**Align** places the lines across the box: *Left*, *Center*, *Right*, or *Justify*. Justified
text stretches every line out to both edges by widening the gaps **between words** — the
letters keep their own spacing — and leaves the last line of each paragraph at its natural
width, the way a printed column does. A line holding a single long word is left alone, since
there is no gap to widen. It needs a width
to fill, so choosing it on a hugging label turns the label's current width into the box's
width (*Auto H*): nothing moves yet, but drag the box narrower — or keep typing — and the
lines wrap and fill it.

**Vertical** places the block down the box: *Top*, *Middle*, or *Bottom*. The box itself never
moves or changes size — only the text inside it does. There is nothing to see until the box is
taller than the text, so this row appears with *Fixed* sizing (a hugging box is exactly as tall
as its text). It is what lines a label up with the middle of the panel beside it.

**Line height** is the distance between lines, as a multiple of the font size (1.2 by default —
1.5 reads more airily, 1 sets the lines tight). **Paragraph space** adds extra room before each
new paragraph, so you can separate paragraphs without leaving blank lines; it counts only where
you pressed Enter, never between the lines of one wrapped paragraph. **Tracking** is letter
spacing — the space added after every letter. Both are in **points**, like the font size, and a
negative tracking pulls letters together. Tracking changes how much fits on a line, so a
wrapping box re-wraps as you adjust it.

**Italic for one word, not the whole box.** Double-click the text to edit it, select the part
you want — a species name, a gene symbol, a single letter — and press **Ctrl+I**, **Ctrl+B** or
**Ctrl+U**. Only that stretch changes; the box keeps its own font, so the rest of the label is
untouched. With nothing selected, while you are typing, the same keys style only what you type
next: press **Ctrl+I**, type the species name, press **Ctrl+I** again and carry on upright. Moving
the cursor or clicking ends that. To style the whole box, click the box without editing it, or
select all of its text first. The formatting sticks to the letters it was given: type in the middle of an italic word and the
new letters are italic too, type against its edge and they are not, and deleting the word takes
its formatting with it. The formatting shows on the canvas as you work. Bold makes letters
wider, so after a bold word the text cursor can sit a few pixels off the letters. In the rare
case where a bold word pushes text onto another line, the box shows plain text while you type,
and the bold appears when you click away. (**Escape** throws the whole edit away, formatting
included.)

**Superscript and subscript.** Select the characters and press **Ctrl++** (superscript) or
**Ctrl+=** (subscript), or use the Inspector's **X²** and **X₂** buttons. The characters are set
smaller and raised or lowered, so *x²* and *H₂O* stay in one text box. **Ctrl+.** and **Ctrl+,**
do the same, as in Google Docs. Pressing the same one again puts the characters back on the line,
and with nothing selected it applies to what you type next, like the other styles.

**Color and the Inspector work on the selected letters too.** While letters are selected, the
Inspector's Text section says *Styling N selected characters*. Its **B**, **I** and **U** buttons
then format just those letters, and you can press several in a row. The *Text* color swatch
paints just those letters as well, so one symbol can be red inside a black label. Click
**Whole box**, or click the canvas, to style the whole text again. A colormap gradient always
covers the whole box, so it is not offered for a few selected letters.

All of these sit in the Inspector's Text section and in the **F** menu, they apply to every
selected text at once, and each adjustment is one undo step. A **named text style** (the
Inspector's *Style* row) carries them too, so "Panel body, justified, 1.4 line height" becomes
one click on every label in the figure — and editing the style restyles every text linked to
it.

## Cascade {#cascade}

Select several things and press **Ctrl+Shift+C**: the **cascade** popover applies a *stepped
delta* across the selection — each object offset a bit more than the last. Pick the property
(position, rotation, opacity, size, stroke width, font size, or a color), the step (add or
multiply), and the ordering (selection, layers, left→right, top→bottom); colors ramp
perceptually in OKLCh (ΔL/ΔC/ΔH per step). The preview is live; **Enter** applies as one undo
step, **Escape** puts everything back. Fanned annotations, graded palettes, staircase layouts —
one gesture.

## Reusable designs {#reusable-designs}

**Ctrl+P** opens your **preset library** — a personal, machine-global collection of styled
shapes, arrows, callouts, and whole groups (a badge, a labelled bracket), organized in folders,
inserted with a click. Save anything from the **F** menu's *save as preset*; a group preset
arrives as one unit you can move as one or ungroup.
